title: Common Cold Overview and Care
excerpt: The common cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. Most people recover in 7 to 10 days. Supportive measures include getting plenty of rest, drinking fluids such as water and warm broth, and using saline nasal sprays. Seek medical care if symptoms worsen after 10 days or if severe high fever develops.

title: Fever in Adults and Home Support
excerpt: A fever is a temporary increase in body temperature, often due to an infection. Staying well hydrated, resting in a comfortable room, and wearing light clothing help reduce discomfort. Seek prompt medical evaluation if a fever exceeds 103°F (39.4°C), lasts longer than 3 days, or is accompanied by a stiff neck, confusion, or difficulty breathing.

title: Sore Throat (Pharyngitis) Care
excerpt: Most sore throats are caused by viral infections such as colds. Gargling with warm salt water (half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water), sipping warm herbal teas with honey, and using a cool-mist humidifier can soothe irritation. Consult a healthcare provider if swallowing becomes extremely difficult or if symptoms persist beyond one week.

title: Tension and Mild Headache Guidance
excerpt: Tension-type headaches are the most common form of headache, typically felt as a dull, steady ache around the forehead or back of the head. Relief strategies include resting in a quiet, dimly lit room, applying a cool or warm compress to the forehead or neck, and staying hydrated. Seek emergency medical care if a headache is sudden, explosive, or accompanied by weakness or vision changes.

title: Acute Cough Overview and Relief
excerpt: A cough helps clear irritants and mucus from the airways. Acute viral coughs often improve with warm fluids, honey (for individuals over 1 year of age), and breathing moist air from a humidifier or shower. Seek medical care if coughing up blood, if coughing lasts longer than 3 weeks, or if accompanied by chest pain or wheezing.

title: Seasonal Allergies (Hay Fever) Management
excerpt: Seasonal allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, nasal congestion, and itchy, watery eyes when exposed to airborne pollen or mold. Keeping windows closed during peak pollen counts, showering after outdoor activity, and using saline nasal rinses help minimize allergen exposure. Consult an allergist or doctor if symptoms interfere with sleep or daily activities.

title: Daily Hydration and Fluid Balance
excerpt: Water is essential for temperature regulation, digestion, joint lubrication, and nutrient delivery throughout the body. Healthy adults should drink fluids regularly throughout the day, aiming for pale clear urine as an indicator of adequate hydration. Requirements increase during physical exertion, warm weather, or episodes of illness.

title: Healthy Sleep Habits (Sleep Hygiene)
excerpt: Most adults need between 7 and 9 hours of quality sleep per night for optimal immune and cognitive health. Good sleep hygiene includes maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, keeping the bedroom dark, quiet, and cool, avoiding screens 30 minutes before bed, and limiting caffeine in the afternoon.

title: Mild Stomach Upset and Indigestion
excerpt: Indigestion (dyspepsia) involves discomfort or a feeling of burning in the upper abdomen, often occurring after eating. Eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding late-night snacking, limiting fatty or spicy foods, and remaining upright for at least two hours after eating can reduce symptoms. Seek emergency care if stomach pain radiates to the jaw, neck, or arm.

title: Nausea and Vomiting Self-Care
excerpt: Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms of gastrointestinal viral illness or dietary intolerance. Managing nausea involves taking small sips of clear liquids such as water, broth, or oral rehydration solutions once vomiting subsides. Transition to bland foods like toast or crackers when ready. Seek medical attention if unable to keep fluids down for 24 hours or if signs of severe dehydration appear.

title: Mild Diarrhea and Oral Rehydration
excerpt: Acute diarrhea is commonly caused by viral or bacterial gastroenteritis. The primary goal is preventing dehydration by drinking oral rehydration solutions, diluted fruit juices, or broths with adequate electrolytes. Avoid dairy, high-sugar beverages, and greasy foods until bowel movements normalize. Consult a doctor if stools contain blood or if high fever occurs.

title: Constipation Prevention and Relief
excerpt: Constipation is defined as having fewer than three bowel movements a week or having hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass. Increasing dietary fiber from whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and fruits alongside drinking sufficient water helps soften stools. Regular physical activity also stimulates healthy bowel motility.

title: Minor Cuts and Scrapes First Aid
excerpt: Minor cuts and abrasions should be rinsed gently with cool tap water and mild soap to remove debris. Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth to stop minor bleeding, apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly, and cover with a sterile bandage. Seek professional care if the wound is deep, gaping, contaminated with soil, or showing signs of infection.

title: First-Degree Minor Burn Care
excerpt: First-degree burns affect only the outer skin layer, causing redness and mild pain without blistering. Immediately hold the burned area under cool running water for 10 to 15 minutes; never apply ice, butter, or oil to a burn. Keep the area clean and apply aloe vera gel or moisturizer. Seek emergency care for burns covering large areas, burns on the face, hands, or joints, or if blisters form.

title: Sunburn Treatment and UV Safety
excerpt: Sunburn is skin damage caused by ultraviolet radiation from sunlight. Soothe sunburned skin with cool baths, damp compresses, and gentle moisturizers containing aloe vera. Drink extra water to avoid dehydration. Prevent future damage by applying broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and wearing protective clothing.

title: Insect Bites and Stings Relief
excerpt: Most mosquito and small insect bites produce mild local swelling, redness, and itching. Wash the bite site with soap and water, then apply a cold ice pack wrapped in a cloth for 10 minutes to reduce swelling. Calamine lotion or hydrocortisone cream can alleviate itching. Seek immediate emergency care if facial swelling, difficulty breathing, or dizziness develops.

title: Heat Exhaustion Prevention and Care
excerpt: Heat exhaustion occurs when the body overheats in hot conditions, causing heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, and cool, pale skin. Immediately move to a shaded or air-conditioned area, loosen tight clothing, and sip cool water. If vomiting occurs or confusion develops, it may be life-threatening heat stroke—call emergency services immediately.

title: Sprains, Strains, and RICE Protocol
excerpt: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, while a strain involves muscles or tendons. For mild sprains, follow the RICE protocol for the first 48 hours: Rest the injured joint, Ice with a cloth-wrapped cold pack for 15-20 minutes at a time, Compress gently with an elastic bandage, and Elevate the limb above heart level. Consult a physician if unable to bear any weight.

title: Stress Management Basics for Health
excerpt: Chronic psychological stress can negatively impact blood pressure, digestion, and sleep patterns. Effective self-care strategies include daily deep diaphragmatic breathing exercises, engaging in moderate physical activity like walking, setting realistic daily priorities, and staying socially connected with supportive friends and family.

title: Eye Strain and Digital Screen Fatigue
excerpt: Extended use of digital devices can cause eye fatigue, dryness, and mild blurring. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, pause and look at an object at least 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. Ensure room lighting minimizes screen glare and blink frequently to replenish the eye's natural tear film.

title: Non-Specific Acute Back Pain Care
excerpt: Most acute lower back pain is caused by muscle strain or ligament sprain and resolves within a few weeks. Gentle movement, avoiding prolonged bed rest, and applying warm or cold packs can relieve stiffness. Consult a doctor immediately if back pain is accompanied by loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin, or weakness in the legs.

title: Hand Hygiene and Infection Prevention
excerpt: Washing hands thoroughly with soap and clean running water for at least 20 seconds is one of the single most effective ways to prevent the spread of infectious illnesses. Wash before eating, after using the restroom, and after blowing your nose, coughing, or touching public surfaces.

title: Physical Activity Basics for Health
excerpt: Public health guidelines recommend that adults aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) per week, alongside muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. Regular movement improves cardiovascular stamina, regulates blood sugar, and supports mental well-being.

title: Balanced Nutrition and Dietary Basics
excerpt: A nutritious diet emphasizes a colorful variety of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy unsaturated fats while limiting added sugars, saturated fats, and excess sodium. Eating balanced meals provides sustained energy, supports gut microbiota, and lowers the long-term risk of chronic metabolic conditions.

title: Recognizing When to Seek Emergency Care
excerpt: Immediate emergency medical attention (calling local emergency services such as 911 in North America, 112 in Europe and India, 999 in the UK, or visiting the nearest emergency department) is essential for sudden severe chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke (facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech), loss of consciousness, heavy uncontrolled bleeding, or sudden severe head trauma. For non-life-threatening concerns, consult a primary care physician.
